extracted.intended_audience: essayists, creative writers, and literary critics interested in rhetorical style, paradox, and moral argument
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing forceful, paradox-embracing essays and moral/creative prose that balance extremes, maintain a fixed vision, and favor precise, dramatic expression over vague metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep contradictory elements side by side (embrace paradox)
rubrics_metrics.description: By defining its main doctrine, the Church not only kept seemingly inconsistent things side by side, but, what was more, allowed them to break out in a sort of artistic violence otherwise possible only to anarchists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present and preserve opposing ideas together rather than smoothing them into a bland compromise. Let contradictory passions (optimism and pessimism, pride and compassion, meekness and fierceness) coexist in your prose to create tension and vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatic extremes rather than bland moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meekness grew more dramatic than madness...Poetry could be acted as well as composed. This heroic and monumental manner in ethics has entirely vanished with supernatural religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vivid, extreme characterization and theatrical moral scenes to mild, moderate statements. Drama and monumental gestures in depiction produce greater moral and aesthetic force than restrained, bland writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinct, pure contrasts instead of diluted mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity sought in most of these cases to keep two colours coexistent but pure. It is not a mixture like russet or purple; it is rather like a shot silk...shot silk is always at right angles, and is in the pattern of the cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep competing elements or tones clearly differentiated (like red and white), rather than blending them into an indistinct gray. Contrast preserves interest and moral clarity in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple types/approaches to coexist (don't force synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church preferred to use its Supermen and to use its Tolstoyans. There must be SOME good in the life of battle...There must be SOME good in the idea of non-resistance...All that the Church did...was to prevent either of these good things from ousting the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the value of different, even opposed, perspectives and include them without co-opting one into the other. In character and argument, permit varied modes to exist rather than ironing them into a single doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show enacted vividness rather than merely advocate reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ethical teachers write reasonably for prison reform; but we are not likely to see Mr. Cadbury...go into Reading Gaol and embrace the strangled corpse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, shocking, or dramatic images and actions to make moral points; avoid abstract, timid advocacy that never demonstrates its convictions in vivid scene or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints and strict rules fuel dramatic creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A strict rule is not only necessary for ruling; it is also necessary for rebelling...This fixed and familiar ideal is necessary to any sort of revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear constraints or a fixed ideal in order to produce decisive, energetic writing. Rules give the writer a stable platform from which to rebel or innovate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms precisely; small slips in phrasing matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines had to be defined within strict limits...A sentence phrased wrong about the nature of symbolism would have broken all the best statues in Europe. A slip in the definitions might stop all the dances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be exact in definitions and phrasing; minor verbal imprecision can undermine entire arguments or tonal effects. Precision preserves the intended consequences of an idea in narrative or essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear abstract statements over vague physical metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: No one will deny that [Nietzsche] was a poetical and suggestive thinker; but he was quite the reverse of strong. He never put his own meaning before himself in bald abstract words...Nietzsche always escaped a question by a physical metaphor...No one will deny that he was a poetical and suggestive thinker; but he was quite the reverse of strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making philosophical or moral claims, state them directly in abstract, unambiguous terms rather than hiding them behind physical metaphors (e.g., 'higher', 'over-man'). Clear wording shows intellectual bravery and prevents evasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold a fixed, enduring vision or ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: This, therefore, is our first requirement about the ideal towards which progress is directed; it must be fixed...The question therefore becomes this: How can we keep the artist discontented with his pictures while preventing him from being vitally discontented with his art?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to a stable vision or ideal as the anchor of creative work. Changing the ideal too frequently renders efforts fruitless; steadiness allows cumulative progress and meaningful reform in art and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make ideals actionable and specific (so action can be swift)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must at any given moment be an abstract right and wrong if any blow is to be struck; there must be something eternal if there is to be anything sudden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate ideals concretely enough that they permit decisive action or dramatic narrative agency. Vague, shifting ideals prevent sudden, effective change in plot, argument, or moral stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the artist discontented with works but faithful to the art
rubrics_metrics.description: How can we make a man always dissatisfied with his work, yet always satisfied with working?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage continual revision and striving in individual pieces while preserving commitment to a chosen artform or methodology; this tension drives productive creativity without dissolving purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive moral or artistic ideals from Nature as authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The main point of Christianity was this: that Nature is not our mother: Nature is our sister...We can be proud of her beauty, since we have the same father; but she has no authority over us; we have to admire, but not to imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'nature' as a blanket justification for artistic or moral norms. Admire and use natural imagery, but do not let naturalistic metaphors dictate what is right or beautiful in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine incongruous traits to produce interest in character and moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Becket wore a hair shirt under his gold and crimson...Becket got the benefit of the hair shirt while the people in the street got the benefit of the crimson and gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create compelling characters and moral tableaux by juxtaposing unexpected traits (humility + splendour, severity + pity). Such contrasts make figures richer and scenes more memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perpetual change of aesthetic or moral ideals (against fashionable fickleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If he altered his favourite colour every day, he would not get on at all...The average modern thinker...will always change his mind...The only thing that remains after all the philosophies is the factory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the tendency to adopt new fashions of thought at every turn. Consistency in core ideals yields lasting work and cumulative achievement; ephemeral shifts produce no durable art.
